entry.title: Reframe: David Sheldon-Hicks and Art Tindsley open a new podcast with Patrice Vermette
entry.summary: David Sheldon-Hicks has spent 16 years designing the futures other people film. The founder of Territory Studio, the team behind screen graphics for Blade Runner 2049 and Dune , now has a microphone of his own. With Art Tindsley, founder of the creative technology agency Pogo, he...
entry.content:
David Sheldon-Hicks has spent 16 years designing the futures other people film. The founder of Territory Studio, the team behind screen graphics for Blade Runner 2049 and Dune, now has a microphone of his own. With Art Tindsley, founder of the creative technology agency Pogo, he has launched Reframe, a podcast about the place where creativity and technology meet.

The show starts from a simple conviction: “the medium is never neutral.” Every tool, from the cave wall to the algorithm, shapes the story told through it. Sheldon-Hicks and Tindsley refuse the old split between artistic intuition and technical logic, and they go looking for the makers, engineers and visionaries who work where the two overlap.

By his own account, Sheldon-Hicks was not sold at first. When Tindsley proposed the idea, he wondered what one more podcast could add to a crowded field. The answer is in the title. Asked constantly whether AI will take creative jobs, Tindsley has written that he prefers a different question: “what creative opportunity exists today that didn’t exist yesterday?”

The first episode sets the bar high. The 39-minute conversation with Patrice Vermette, the Oscar-winning production designer of Dune, Arrival and Sicario, covers his long partnership with Denis Villeneuve, why a set should work as a character rather than “empty calories,” and how limits tend to produce the best ideas. It is a conversation between people who have built worlds side by side. Territory designed screen graphics for Villeneuve’s Dune, and Sheldon-Hicks and Vermette have shared a stage at SXSW London.

Reframe is out now on Apple Podcasts, and listeners can send in a voicemail for a chance to be heard on a future episode. One episode in, the premise is clear, and so is the ambition. We will be listening.

entry.content:
Industry veteran joins the integrated creative company from Hornet to build long-term client partnerships with ambitious brands.

Perfect Stranger, the global integrated creative company from Hornet, announced the appointment of Tony Kadillak as Head of Client Partnerships on October 5, 2026. Kadillak will work alongside Perfect Stranger’s leadership team to support the continued growth of the company’s global client base.

Tony Kadillak, Head of Client Partnerships at Perfect Stranger. Image supplied by Perfect Stranger / Red Setter.

The appointment reunites Kadillak with Perfect Stranger Executive Creative Director Daniel Fries. The two worked together from 2010 to 2014 at Leroy & Clarkson, the Emmy-winning design and branding agency Fries founded in 2001. Kadillak brings more than 20 years’ experience in the creative sector and co-founded Assembly, a networking event for entertainment and brand marketers.

Kadillak will focus on brands that want their marketing to move the business and are ready to invest in long-term builds to get there. From startups and challengers to established brands, Perfect Stranger works directly with CMOs and brand leaders across the full stack, from brand strategy and positioning through design, animation and production to develop the creative needed to cut through in today’s noisy marketplace.

Kadillak says: “This is a relationships business, and who you go into battle with matters as much as the work itself. I learned so much working with Daniel and the team he assembled that I couldn’t pass up the chance to do it again. Combine Perfect Stranger’s energy and ambition with the legacy and foundation of Hornet, and it was an easy decision.”

Fries adds: “Tony has always had a hunger for bigger, more strategic challenges, and he’s a people person through and through. You can win a job in the room with the right work, but it’s chemistry and trust that keep clients for the long term. Tony brings exactly the type of thoughtful, creative partnership that we want to nurture at Perfect Stranger.”

Perfect Stranger launched in 2026 as a sister company to Hornet, combining agency-level strategic thinking with Hornet’s 25 years of global production expertise. Kadillak’s appointment supports the company’s ambition to expand its strategic, creative, and business development capabilities, creating new opportunities for collaboration and long-term client partnerships.

About Perfect Stranger

Perfect Stranger is a full-stack creative company, offering brand, advertising, design, animation and production through a fully integrated model with sister company, Hornet. Created in response to demand for more agile creative partners, the company helps ambitious brands in verticals including enterprise technology, media, and consulting, move seamlessly from strategy and positioning to campaign development and execution across global markets. Visit perfectstranger.co for more.

entry.title: Lofsöng and the Language That Outlives Us
entry.summary: Editor’s note by Carlos El Asmar Jesse went to Tribeca and came back with a haunted hotel that sings . Now he has brought us singing stones, a shapeshifting piece of origami, and a question about how to speak to people who might exist 100,000 years from now. I’m beginning to see ...
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player

Editor’s note by Carlos El Asmar

Jesse went to Tribeca and came back with a haunted hotel that sings. Now he has brought us singing stones, a shapeshifting piece of origami, and a question about how to speak to people who might exist 100,000 years from now. I’m beginning to see a pattern.

What draws me to Lofsöng is the trust it places in the person on the other side of the screen. A shape, a vibration, a patch of light can ask us to stop and work something out for ourselves. I love that. So much of our working life is spent making sure the message lands immediately. Here is a world willing to let us be a little lost.

For this next chapter of our Tribeca coverage, Jesse speaks with Unrelated Studio’s Alessandro Durando about the ideas behind that world, and the people who helped him build it. Put your headphones on for this one. The stones have something to say.

On an afternoon at Pier 57, somewhere between the chatter of a dozen playable demos and the steady flow of visitors through the Tribeca Games Gallery, I found myself in front of a screen that refused to speak. No dialogue. No map. No subtitles. Only a small figure in an oversized helmet crossing a gray desert of dust, an origami companion folding itself into the wind, and enormous concrete monuments waiting to be heard.

That game is LOFSÖNG, a world premiere in the 2026 Tribeca Games official selection, developed by Unrelated Studio, a team based in Turin, Italy. Its creative director, Alessandro Durando, sat down with me to explain how a nuclear waste repository in Finland, the idea of speaking architecture, and a Sardinian sculptor who taught stones to sing all ended up inside the same piece of software.

You explore by listening, singing to sculptures, and discovering how mechanisms respond. Your origami companion reshapes itself to carry you across the Dust Sea, becoming a kite, a glider, a sailboat, and new forms appear as the world opens up. Meaning arrives through what you do and what the world gives back.

Lofsöng at the Tribeca Games gallery, Pier 57, New York. Photo: Jesse Rylander.

A message built to outlast language

The game, Durando told me, begins with a question. How can we, as humanity, communicate with the future?

The seed of that question is a real place. In Finland, deep in the bedrock, sits Onkalo, a repository built for the long-term disposal of spent nuclear fuel. Its name comes from the Finnish word for a cavity in rock. The timescale, reaching far beyond the lives of any of us, would not let Durando go. If a structure has to outlive every language spoken on Earth today, how do you warn whoever finds it that what lies inside can kill them?

“They tried to come up with how to communicate without languages or signs. And essentially the game starts with this.”
Alessandro Durando

Buildings that say their own names

The first answer Durando found was architecture. Brutalism is the obvious reference in LOFSÖNG, with its raw concrete, impossible scale, and forms that feel less built than excavated. He also drew on architecture parlante, or "speaking architecture." The idea is that a building can announce its identity and purpose through form alone, without a single written word.

It is a beautiful idea, and Durando is the first to admit its limits.

“Of course, it’s not enough, talking just with architecture.”
Alessandro Durando

A wall can tell you it is a wall. It cannot tell you why it was raised, or what it cost the people who raised it. So he went looking for a second language.

Lofsöng, a traveler among monumental concrete forms. Courtesy of Unrelated Studio.

Stones that sing

He found it in Sardinia, in the work of Pinuccio Sciola. The late sculptor spent decades carving basalt and limestone with precise incisions that turned solid rock into instruments. His pietre sonore, or sound stones, are lithophones that resonate when touched or rubbed.

For Durando, Sciola’s stones cracked the whole project open. If a rock can sing, then sound itself could be the universal language he was searching for.

“Sound is mathematics and numbers.”
Alessandro Durando

The possibility of translating vibrations into patterns became a foundation for the game’s wordless world.

That logic runs through the sculptures and mechanisms you encounter. They are instruments, each with its own behavior. Some answer like the stone lithophones, others like enormous pipes. Even the protagonist’s own voice is part of the orchestra. The Tribeca demo did not yet have an original score, Durando told me, but sound was never absent, and sometimes its omission spoke just as loudly.

In LOFSÖNG, sound is not something laid over the picture at the end of the pipeline. It is the grammar the picture is built on.

Lofsöng, sound and geometry meet in a stone instrument. Courtesy of Unrelated Studio.

Seven future humanities and the weight of memory

LOFSÖNG is set so far ahead that the word "future" starts to feel too small. Languages have changed beyond recognition. Civilizations have collapsed. Humanity itself has been replaced, more than once. In Durando’s mythology, we sapiens are only the first humanity, and seven more come after us.

Each of them left monuments behind, and each monument holds that civilization’s memories, including its mistakes. The protagonist belongs to the last of these humanities, the only one still walking the Earth. As you play, you find the monuments one by one and, piece by piece, assemble a song from them. That song opens the gate to the final monument, the one built by her own people.

The title carries that idea. Durando described the song at the heart of Lofsöng as an elegy for something that is gone. The game, in other words, is you composing a eulogy for every humanity that came before you, including ours.

But Durando was clear that this is not nostalgia.

“The main thing about the game is not the importance of memory, but what you can do with the memory of sapiens.”
Alessandro Durando

He pointed out that we tend to forget within ten or twenty years, even as we try to imagine ourselves thousands of years ahead. The real question, for him, is what we do with the weight of knowing what went wrong, and whether we use it to stop repeating the same mistakes.

There are no written words to guide you through any of this, and that is a deliberate act of trust.

“We want to respect the intelligence of the player.”
Alessandro Durando

You connect the dots yourself, and the meaning you build is yours.

Lofsöng, patterns spread across a platform beneath a monument. Courtesy of Unrelated Studio.

Grain, decay, and a Geiger compass

Watching the footage, I told Durando it looked like a dream, and it reminded me of a tale from my childhood called Ratatatam, a story told in many languages with that same open, otherworldly sense of space. He agreed that the familiarity is part of the design.

The most striking choice, for me, is the grain. It covers everything, and Durando sees it as doing two jobs at once. On one level, it is material, the rough, porous skin of brutalist concrete. On another, it is decay. This is a dead world, saturated with radiation, and the image is meant to feel like an old photograph that has been disturbed and ruined by it.

The same thinking shapes how the protagonist moves through it. She speaks only through vocalization, and her voice works almost like a Geiger compass, helping her read the decay around her and find her way. Her humanity has learned to endure this harsh place, but the place itself stays eerie and hard to grasp. Durando wants players to feel that tension constantly, to look at a mechanism and wonder what it is and what it is for.

“The game tries to prime the curiosity of the player, like a child in a way.”
Alessandro Durando

You experiment, and the world answers.

Lofsöng, the traveler and origami companion cross the Dust Sea. Courtesy of Unrelated Studio.

Years in the head, six months on the screen

The story of these humanities lived in Durando’s head for years before it became a game. He imagined it as a short film, then as something that could grow into a TV series. In the end, he chose games because he believes they are one of the best media for this particular story, one where the audience has to discover meaning instead of receiving it.

Turning that story into a game concept took a few months. The first version of the demo, he admitted, was completely different from what Tribeca audiences played, and it simply did not work. So he put the project on hiatus.

What brought it back was finding the right team, people who could finally build the vision he had carried from the beginning. The demo at Pier 57 represented six months of production.

I find that part of the story quietly encouraging. Every artist I know has a project sitting in a drawer, shelved after a first attempt that missed. Sometimes an idea is waiting for the right collaborators.

Players at the Tribeca Games gallery, Pier 57, New York. Photo: Jesse Rylander.

A player willing to listen

When I asked what gamers will find new here, Durando laughed that it is up to them. But he has watched people react to the trailer and the demo, and the response tends to land in the same place. The game feels familiar and unique at once. Players mention Journey, Monument Valley, and Shadow of the Colossus, especially in its desolate, monumental landscapes.

The uniqueness, he believes, comes from where the ideas were born. Onkalo, architecture parlante, and Sciola’s stones all come from outside games, and that gives LOFSÖNG an aesthetic and a world that do not feel borrowed.

His goal is not to teach anyone a lesson.

“to leave you something emotionally after you finish it.”
Alessandro Durando

I keep coming back to Onkalo, and to the problem of building something for a future we cannot picture. Durando’s answer to that impossible problem is not a better sign. It is a song, and a player willing to listen.

Lofsöng is in development, with its release date still to be announced. The studio lists Steam, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox on PC, and PlayStation 5 as planned platforms.

entry.title: Haymaker VFX Acquires SWISS
entry.summary: Stockholm-based, globally recognized creative team becomes part of Haymaker VFX in next phase of the studio’s international growth. GOTHENBURG, SWEDEN – 1 October 2026 – Haymaker VFX has acquired Swedish visual effects studio SWISS, bringing together two long-established names in...
entry.content:
Stockholm-based, globally recognized creative team becomes part of Haymaker VFX in next phase of the studio’s international growth.

GOTHENBURG, SWEDEN – 1 October 2026 – Haymaker VFX has acquired Swedish visual effects studio SWISS, bringing together two long-established names in high-end VFX to strengthen Haymaker’s creative and production presence in Stockholm. The acquisition forms part of Haymaker VFX’s wider growth strategy as the studio expands its capacity and international reach across advertising, entertainment, and immersive experiences.

Founded by Alex Hansson, Haymaker VFX has built a strong position across high-end advertising and entertainment, with operations in Gothenburg and Los Angeles and now an expanding presence in Stockholm. Its North American operation, led by Leslie Sorrentino, provides a local base for the studio’s growing relationships with agencies, production companies and entertainment clients across the market. Haymaker VFX has recorded three consecutive years of growth, with revenue increasing by approximately 57% between 2024 and 2025, as its international client base and project work have expanded. Recent work includes Amazon Prime’s Fallout – Season 2 and The Wizard of Oz at Sphere.

SWISS, established in 2002, has built an exceptional reputation in visual effects and animation, working with leading directors, agencies, production companies and brands internationally. Particularly well known for its work in high-end advertising, its work includes Volvo Trucks’ The Epic Split, winner of two Grand Prix at Cannes Lions. Their artists and creative talent now join Haymaker VFX, adding significant creative depth and capacity to its Stockholm operation.

The SWISS brand will remain, preserving more than two decades of creative heritage and industry recognition. The two companies also share a strong cultural fit, with a common focus on craft, creative ambition and close collaboration.

Alongside its creative capabilities, Haymaker VFX has invested extensively in technology and pipeline development, integrating new tools – including AI – where they can improve creative and production workflows.

“SWISS has built an internationally respected brand, body of work, and team over more than twenty years. We share the same passion for craft, creative ambition and close collaboration, which makes this a very natural fit. Bringing our strengths together gives Haymaker VFX greater creative depth and capacity at a time when we are ready to accelerate our international growth and take on more of the world’s most demanding projects, while staying true to the boutique model that defines us.” – Alex Hansson, Founder and CEO, Haymaker VFX

“North America remains a major growth market for Haymaker VFX. Clients increasingly want partners that can stay close and responsive while still having the depth to handle larger, more complex scopes. The addition of SWISS strengthens what we can offer those clients without changing the way we work with them.” – Leslie Sorrentino, President, North America, Haymaker VFX

“SWISS has always been about craft, creative ambition and the people behind the work. Joining Haymaker VFX gives our team the opportunity to build on that heritage as part of a broader international platform with the same creative values.” – Erik Holmedal, SWISS

About Haymaker VFX

Founded by Alex Hansson, Haymaker VFX is an independent visual effects studio working across advertising, entertainment and immersive experiences. With operations in Gothenburg and Los Angeles and an expanding presence in Stockholm, the studio combines high-end visual effects and creative talent with a technology-led approach to production. Recent work includes Amazon Prime’s Fallout – Season 2 and The Wizard of Oz at Sphere. Haymaker VFX works with international studios, brands, agencies and production partners while maintaining the collaborative, boutique model on which the company was built. https://www.haymakerfx.com/

About SWISS

Founded in Stockholm in 2002, SWISS is an internationally recognised visual effects and animation studio with deep roots in high-end advertising. Over more than two decades, the studio has collaborated with leading directors, agencies, production companies and brands in Sweden and internationally. Its body of work includes Volvo Trucks’ The Epic Split. Following its acquisition by Haymaker VFX, the SWISS brand will remain, with its creative talent and heritage joining the wider Haymaker VFX team. https://swiss.se/

entry.summary: What happens when the tools of the game become the game? That was the question driving this new 3D animation Laundry created as part of a sweeping promotional campaign for Logitech’s latest G3 series. The challenge wasn’t just to showcase a mouse, keyboard, and headset, but to tr...
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player

What happens when the tools of the game become the game? That was the question driving this new 3D animation Laundry created as part of a sweeping promotional campaign for Logitech’s latest G3 series. The challenge wasn’t just to showcase a mouse, keyboard, and headset, but to transform them into characters with presence, personality, and purpose. Each piece of gear was given its own unique abilities and strengths to show how they work together to bring players the best experience possible. Laundry took extra care to find some of those exciting gaming moments that makes viewers feel something rather than simply listing off specs.

The real creative puzzle was building a world that felt alive and eclectic without ever losing the thread of the brand. Using the client’s design language as our palette, we constructed environments that were bold and surprising at every turn, yet unmistakably cohesive. A gaming world that could shift in tone and texture from scene to scene, but always felt like it belonged to the same universe. The end result was an animated campaign that elevates and mythologizes the product line. When you design a world around that idea, it doesn’t just grab attention, it pulls players in!

entry.title: Art Director Flora MacLeod Joins Electric Theatre Collective
entry.summary: Art director Flora MacLeod has joined Electric Theatre Collective , bringing a practice that connects tactile CG imagery with an interest in the natural world. She joins the studio’s growing 3D design team, working with Will Denning and James Britton on projects across technology...
entry.content:
Art director Flora MacLeod has joined Electric Theatre Collective, bringing a practice that connects tactile CG imagery with an interest in the natural world. She joins the studio’s growing 3D design team, working with Will Denning and James Britton on projects across technology, beauty and fashion.

At Optical Arts, MacLeod contributed to Channel 4’s 2023 idents and worked on product animations for Dyson, Aveda and Bowers & Wilkins, collaborating with Fabrice Le Nezet and Dan Tobin Smith. Her Hidden Life project at Outernet London turned the world of plankton into an immersive environment spanning five walls and four storeys.

“I have always been really invested in the emotive side of creative work and love when visuals meet sound and story,” MacLeod says. At ETC, she will work within a small design team connected to the studio’s wider VFX and colour departments.

Strategy director James Britton describes her arrival as the next chapter for the team, pointing to her tactile approach and sense of aesthetics.

entry.title: Maxon’s Fall 2026 Release Adds Cinema 4D Scatter and Liquid FX
entry.summary: Maxon has released its Fall 2026 updates, introducing the 2027.0 versions of Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Redshift, Red Giant and Autograph. Announced on October 14, the release adds tools for building dense environments, extending liquid simulations and moving work between applications. O...
entry.content:
Maxon has released its Fall 2026 updates, introducing the 2027.0 versions of Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Redshift, Red Giant and Autograph. Announced on October 14, the release adds tools for building dense environments, extending liquid simulations and moving work between applications.

In Cinema 4D, the new Scatter System distributes objects such as vegetation, rocks and debris, with controls for clustering, filtering and transforms. Its connection to MoGraph means artists can use Fields and Effectors to shape and animate those distributions. Liquid FX adds foam, spray and bubbles that respond to an existing liquid simulation.

ZBrush gains a UV Editor with UDIM and texel-density support, plus Selection Sets for saving and recalling masks, Polygroups and other configurations. On iPad, Spotlight and non-destructive 3D Layers extend reference, painting and sculpting workflows.

Maxon says Redshift’s revised memory architecture and interaction updates reduce the delay between scene changes and rendered feedback. The update also introduces procedural fur, fibers, textiles and knitted materials generated at render time. These are the developer’s stated capabilities, rather than results from an independent performance test.

For compositing, Red Giant adds Scene Light, an AI-powered relighting tool for After Effects, while Maxon Noise brings Cinema 4D-style procedural noise into Universe. Autograph gains an optional Model Context Protocol server for connecting supported AI tools to its native workflows, along with a direct Cinema 4D connection for copying supported 3D elements, cameras, lights and animation into the application.

The releases became available on October 14. See Maxon’s full announcement for the feature details.

Created over several years, the film combines procedural animation, 2D and 3D animation, digital compositing and organic visual systems to build an evolving universe of forms, textures and transformations.

entry.title: I’M HAVING A BREAKDOWN: DREAMCAT, the monster that wasn’t his
entry.summary: Editor’s note I cannot tell you how DREAMCAT found me. I don’t have social media, and the morning of our call I was still trying to remember who sent it. What I do remember is the behind-the-scenes video. Something clicked, and when something makes me feel something, I pursue it....
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player

Editor’s note

I cannot tell you how DREAMCAT found me. I don’t have social media, and the morning of our call I was still trying to remember who sent it. What I do remember is the behind-the-scenes video. Something clicked, and when something makes me feel something, I pursue it.

People need to know what happened to this film after the shoot, when the one they thought they had quietly turned into a different one. That is the story a press release cannot tell, and it is the reason this series exists.

When I saw a studio in Düsseldorf and an animator in Brussels spend almost three years on a film combining live action and hand-drawn animation, then throw away two weeks of that drawing because it wasn’t true to the man on screen, I felt something I hadn’t felt in a while. Then I met them, on a Friday night at nine o’clock their time, beers in hand, and I couldn’t believe it either.

This is what I’m Having a Breakdown is for. Danny, Joost and Jakob opened the drawers: the plates, the scrapped monster, the Jedi shot that got cut down, the raw drawings and the finished frames. Here is the film they made, and the one they didn’t.

The making of DREAMCAT. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

The monster that wasn’t his

Joost Jansen had spent roughly two weeks animating a monster for a film about himself. Then he said it did not belong there.

Director Daniel “Danny” Bartels had been bracing for that conversation. Two weeks of drawing were in the cut, and he was still working out how to raise it without hurting his friend. He never had to. After one of the project’s long breaks, it was Joost who came back and said the monster wasn’t working.

DREAMCAT began as a portrait of Joost, made by MAKE MAMI PROUD in Düsseldorf, with live action and his own hand-drawn animation. Danny’s first story was a classic hero’s journey. A dark creature takes over parts of the artist’s life, Joost regains his strength in the woods, and his characters help him defeat it. Dreamcat, the round-headed figure the film is named for, would show up in exactly one shot, the last one, for the rescue.

The December 2023 offline edit was built around a dark demon. Danny had asked for an octopus, something that would get its grip on Joost. Joost drew a slimy hybrid of a moth and an octopus, pink-spotted and tentacled, and brought it to life. Then everyone watched the cut. The monster was revealed too early, it sat in the wrong place in the story, and it had become an insect-spider mix too complex to animate well. Most of all it had nothing to do with Joost.

“I felt that I needed to translate the concept of a ‘demon’ into characters from my own creative universe.”
Joost Jansen

The studio’s first instinct was to swap in something more abstract, a dark smoke creature that could be animated freely and placed anywhere. Joost had a better idea. He went back to his sketchbooks and looked for the characters that kept showing up on their own. There was Dreamcat, of course, always there. There was a woman with a round head, his feminine side. There was a child, the one who opens the film wearing a half-Dreamcat helmet, his inner child. And there was the achievement-driven macho, the boss who chases him about deadlines.

“Each represents an inner voice within me: the child within, my feminine side, and the achievement-driven macho. Each functions as a kind of demon, capable of getting me into trouble or guiding me towards enlightenment.”
Joost Jansen

In March 2024 the monster was scrapped for good. Dreamcat moved from the last shot to the lead role, not the rescuer at the end but the hero beside Joost for the whole film. A story about defeating something foreign became what Joost had always been drawing: a balancing act with the voices in his own head, the ones that fuel him and the ones that overwhelm him, which are the same ones.

“For me, the biggest breakthrough came when I introduced my recurring alter egos into the film. Suddenly, everything fell into place.”
Joost Jansen

DREAMCAT, the abandoned monster in an early forest composite. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

Getting Joost in front of the camera

The name came before the studio. About ten years ago, editor Philipp Schneider proposed MAKE MAMI PROUD as a joke with a dare inside it. When Danny finally founded the company in 2021, with Schneider and producer Isabel Ley, Philipp worried the name was too old. They decided it could still be a promise: if the work was brave enough, the irony would hold.

Danny had come up as a Motion Designer after graduating in 2010, directing VFX-heavy music videos on weekends. He met Jakob Saretz in 2014 at Congaz, and they bonded over those videos and over techno. In 2021 a Dr. Oetker commercial introduced Danny to Joost, a Brussels cel animator who draws, in his words, “to observe, explore, and make sense of the world around me.” Danny remembers a nightmare client and a great time working with Joost. Jakob joined MMP in 2022, working across Motion Design and compositing, and Joost became the studio’s permalancer for the German market.

That first job together also left a character behind. Danny traces DREAMCAT’s sergeant to the creative director on the Dr. Oetker commercial, who kept asking whether the flamingos looked happy enough. As Danny puts it: “Our first shared enemy — and apparently he stayed with us.”

The studio had been making artist portraits for brands the usual way: an interview, a workbench, a voice explaining process. Danny wanted the opposite, a portrait from the inside out, where the artist’s inner world was drawn rather than described. He knew exactly who he wanted to film, and exactly how that person would answer.

“When Daniel first suggested making a film about me, my initial reaction was: What a terrible idea. Why would you want to film me? I’m not that interesting.”
Joost Jansen

So Danny pitched it without the interviews. They would simply visit Joost’s places, the studio, the forest, his happy place in the woods, and let his own characters flood in. One rule governed everything that followed, including the monster: Joost was the client.

“The most important thing for me was that Joost would never feel ashamed or cringe watching the final film. He should feel good seeing himself in it, feel it was honest to who he is, and have the space to express himself.”
Daniel “Danny” Bartels

That was Danny’s test for the film, and it gave Joost’s discomfort with the monster real weight.

Joost trusted him, and somewhere under the reluctance he felt the pull of stepping outside his comfort zone. He said yes. The three of them had ended one drunken night showing each other their personal projects and agreeing the studio needed one of its own. This was it.

Three nights in Brussels

They shot in September 2023: three days in Brussels, mostly at night and in the early morning, plus one underwater day in a pool in Mülheim an der Ruhr. The crew was small and young. MMP is not a film production company, and the shoots it had done before were the easy kind, in a studio, with daylight.

The forest taught them the difference. A lighting setup Danny had budgeted at thirty minutes took four hours. By the time the lights were where they needed to be, the quiet scenes were gone: Joost walking after his run, discovering his demons one at a time, the slow private moments between a man and the characters only he can see.

DREAMCAT, the forest plate, animation pass and final composite. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

Danny remembers leaving the shoot deeply disappointed. They had missed so many of the images he wanted that he wondered whether they could make a film from what remained.

The scene that hurt most was the rescue. Several shots had been planned with a stand-in on set, to be painted over as Dreamcat in post, including one where Dreamcat saves Joost. Those shots became full animation instead, with placeholders dropped into the preview edits. Only when Danny saw a cut with the placeholders in and could imagine how it would play did he believe in the film again.

The bill came later. Danny turned about five planned paint-over shots into full animation, a decision that added roughly ten days of drawing for Joost. His verdict is unsentimental: a larger, more experienced camera and lighting crew would have saved money and frustration. He would only do it again with the right people on board from the start.

The breakdown

Jakob’s job across the whole film was the same: glue live-action plates and hand-drawn animation into one composite, and merge Joost’s style with the footage so the film holds a single look. Joost describes the handoff with less ceremony.

“I throw things at Jakob in a kind of frenzy. My work is often raw and direct, and Jakob knows how to distil it into something more legible and balanced.”
Joost Jansen

The passes make that collaboration visible. A drawing arrives with its own energy. Tracking, focus, color and light decide how that energy lives in the shot.

Joost describes the film this way: “Physical and mental spaces constantly overlap, which gives it a somewhat delirious quality.”

The forest

The film opens in the woods, and the woods had to feel like Joost’s head. Jakob generated a depth pass from the footage with the Quick Depth 3 plugin and matched it to a 3D camera in After Effects, which let him rebuild the depth of field of the entire scene in post. The focus trembles, mirroring Dreamcat’s madness, and because the drawn characters share that focus with the plate, they sit inside it instead of on top of it. Compare the plain comp with the final and watch what happens between the figures and the trees.

“DREAMCAT gave us room to try techniques that tight commercial schedules rarely allow, to push our compositing of cel animation and live action further.”
Jakob Saretz

Joost’s drawing changes approach shot by shot. Some footage is rotoscoped, some illustrations are animated traditionally, and some camera moves are animated or tracked. Where the animation has to lock into the live action he draws on ones, a new drawing for every frame. Where the scene needs balance more than integration, he animates on threes.

“Making this film reminded me once again that I’m not someone who likes taking shortcuts. I feel that I can express myself most authentically through the actual frame-by-frame process.”
Joost Jansen

DREAMCAT, the forest shot in four passes, from live-action plate to final composite. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

The studio

Drawn animation and live-action footage speak different visual languages, because each follows its own logic of light. A character painted in saturated purple needs a relationship with the light on a photographed desk. Jakob’s answer was to make the footage meet the drawings halfway.

“On several shots we used the After Effects plugin to relight the plates so they appeared lit by Joost’s illustrations.”
Jakob Saretz

The plugin was AI Relight. The six stages of this shot follow a sketchbook on Joost’s desk, from the raw plate through the animated illustration, Joost’s character pass, the first comp, the light and glow pass, and the final frame. Watch the paper and the desktop as Dreamcat’s torch flares. The drawn light starts to land on photographed surfaces, and the room responds to something that was never in it.

DREAMCAT, six stages of the sketchbook shot, from the original desk to the final torchlight. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

The ending

The ending they shot had Joost leaving his atelier, walking down the street, and joining his characters in one last wide shot. The camera would pan up to the sky. Title. Credits.

Once the offline edit was locked, Jakob sent Joost the three shots that make up the sequence. The studio painted every sign and piece of trash out of the plates. Joost animated every element of the scene, drawing them flat, 3D-tracking them into the footage himself, and handing it all back as a slap comp in After Effects. Jakob rearranged elements so the viewer wouldn’t get lost, then tracked, masked, tweaked color, glow and depth of field, added a colored zebra crossing to the first shot, and relit the plate so the characters cast light onto the cobblestones.

He was still finishing those three shots when Joost changed the ending.

“The old ending was a classic, old-school film ending: a pan up to the sky, then the credits. It all felt like something we had seen many times before, and we had the sense that it didn’t do the film justice.”
Jakob Saretz

Joost’s replacement is a fighter jet. It bursts out of the street toward the camera with every character aboard, close enough to read their faces.

DREAMCAT, the original sky ending and two frames from the revised plane sequence. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

“Your demons are really your best friends. They are part of you and can be both positive and negative. Enjoy each other, and enjoy yourself.”
Joost Jansen

The idea, design and animation of the plane are entirely Joost’s. Jakob adjusted the colors and added depth of field to guide the eye through a busy scene. The new ending shortened the last wide shot, so the elements he had just placed had to be rearranged once more. The wide shot had made the characters tiny. The plane let the film show their emotions one last time, up close.

DREAMCAT, four versions of the ending, from the street footage to the finished plane sequence. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

The new ending was part of a larger edit Joost made while Jakob was away on three months of parental leave in 2025. Before leaving, Jakob had pushed toward a solid version of the film. When the three of them reviewed Joost’s cut in September, he could see what the break had made possible.

“While I was away, Joost had made a few important tweaks to the edit: a new intro, some new shots, and finally an ending that felt right. I felt new energy and motivation, and the film felt like it was in its final form.”
Jakob Saretz

The edit gave Danny another problem to solve. It had the right mood, but no dramatic arc or real conclusion. The team briefed 2WEI Music, and the composition by Niklas Vinken gave the story the structure it needed. For Danny, it was a goosebump moment: “It made the story work and lifted every emotion we’d been hoping for.”

Making the Jedi shot smaller

One of the most revealing comparisons is a shot they reduced. After Joost comes out of the water with new energy, the team had planned a moment of power in the forest: moonlight, floating rocks, a hero shot built in 3D that they nicknamed the Jedi shot. The work-in-progress runs just under four seconds. The final shot runs 2.4.

DREAMCAT, the finished shot’s opening, the earlier rock effect and the final composite. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

Danny judged the shot by what Joost was feeling at that point in the story.

“It just felt out of place — too much like a show-off 3D shot, candy for a future reel. It wasn’t in the right mood for that moment in the film. It’s a quiet moment of regaining strength and thinking clearly, of finding motivation again. Not a maximum-power moment.”
Daniel “Danny” Bartels

The rocks still float in the finished version. The moment just passes more quickly. A breakdown usually tells you how an effect was built. This one tells you why they pulled it back, and that having made something elaborate did not oblige them to keep it.

DREAMCAT, the earlier Jedi shot and the shorter final cut. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

What “every frame by hand” means here

The project page says it in capitals: NO AI. EVERY FRAME BY HAND. It sits beside a film that uses AI-assisted compositing tools, so I asked the team to define the scope precisely. A claim like that deserves to be checked, and the answer is more interesting than the slogan.

Joost drew the film’s cel animation by hand. Jakob says that, as more of MMP’s client projects involved AI, DREAMCAT became a welcome return to their traditional workflow and to the way Joost works. Along the way they tried quick AI-generated layouts in the edit. Danny remembers the initial excitement fading when the results did not feel authentic to the film.

Where AI does appear in the finished film is in compositing. Jakob identifies AI Relight and Quick Depth as tools used on the shots. His distinction is between that technical processing and generating imagery or animation.

DREAMCAT, the sketchbook before and after the torchlight is added. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

“Every drawn frame in DREAMCAT is made by hand. AI was only used as a technical tool in compositing and never used to generate imagery or animation.”
Jakob Saretz

That statement is about the drawn animation. DREAMCAT also contains live-action photography and 3D work, and saying the whole film was drawn by hand would miss the collaboration the passes show. For Danny, the film had to be recognizable as Joost’s, made in a way that felt true to him. Joost puts it more simply.

“For me it means that a great deal of personal sweat has gone into the film. It is a human, personal film, made through human energy and connection.”
Joost Jansen

What it cost

Studios rarely say what a passion project costs. MMP tracks its time, so Danny opened the books.

Joost worked nearly 50 days on the film, and the studio was able to pay him for half of that time. The team recorded 532 hours excluding Joost, with Jakob’s 190 hours included in that total. The studio made room for the project during paid working hours, while Joost also contributed time it could not cover.

The film fitted into gaps between client projects, which is why there were so many breaks and why some lasted months. Danny says those breaks helped him see when the work was heading in the wrong direction and recover the motivation to change it. Jakob calls it a marathon, not a sprint, with one warning every studio should write down: you cannot run without a finish line forever. Festival submissions finally gave them that deadline. The final online version was delivered in August 2026, almost three years after the shoot.

Danny’s advice is shorter. Just do it. On a tight budget, plan with boards and an animatic so you can see whether it works before you start drawing. Work with people you love working with and know inside out. Talk about it a lot, make it a shared goal, and keep it alive even when it hurts.

Coming out from behind the drawings

On our call, Jakob said something I wrote down: the best way to destroy a good idea is to show it to many people and ask for their opinion. The three kept the creative decisions between them. The rest of the studio got updates, but almost no one saw the film while it was taking shape.

For Joost, the moment that defined it was the shoot he never wanted to do. Playing himself in front of a camera forced him to look at how he presents himself, and how he presents his work in relation to who he is. He calls it confronting and liberating in the same breath, and admits what the film taught him: it would be a shame to stay hidden in the shadows.

For Danny, the stakes were different this time. “I’d done plenty of passion projects on my own in the past, but this was the first under the company flag — so I pushed myself to make it worth it and make it special.”

“After events like OFFF or Us By Night, Jakob, Joost and I always ended up in the same conversation: that we have to push further if we ever want to tell our own success story, and that nobody is going to hand us anything. We have to do it ourselves to build the kind of momentum and attention that might lead somewhere bigger — to a position where we can actually choose which clients and projects we work with, and which we don’t.”
Daniel “Danny” Bartels

They returned to those conversations after hard, high-pressure client jobs, talking about their Dreamcat baby and how to keep feeding it. There were also periods when Danny needed the others to keep it moving.

“And I gained a lot of respect for Jakob and Joost, because they never gave up or lost motivation for this film — even in the periods when I was burned out and had lost mine. It was good that we kept each other going. After finishing it and finally releasing it, we felt satisfied and free in a way none of us had in a long time.”
Daniel “Danny” Bartels

The film is also a message to anyone who has drawn something only to have a client email land on top of it. There is a shot in DREAMCAT where Joost is trying to draw and the feedback pops up and he is simply furious. Jakob’s gloss on it: we feel you, you’re not alone. Everyone walks the two paths, the client work that pays and the work that is yours, and the base of all the other work is the voice you refuse to lose.

I keep coming back to the monster. Two weeks of drawing, and the man who drew it was the one to say it did not belong. That decision gave Joost room to bring more of himself into a film he had barely wanted to appear in. Danny hopes the next passion project might take a year instead of three. The film has given him a reason to want another one.

“I think what makes the film special is that it grew out of a shared desire to create. That spirit should never be lost: find fulfilment in the act of making itself.”
Joost Jansen

And Mami? I asked whether she was proud. Jakob said they were trying. Always.

DREAMCAT, outtakes from the shoot. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen.

entry.title: The Haunted Hotel That Sings Back: Anil Glendinning on There Are No Ghosts at the Grand
entry.summary: Editor’s note: Our Tribeca 2026 coverage continues with Jesse Rylander’s conversation with Anil Glendinning, co-founder and creative director of Friday Sundae , the studio behind There Are No Ghosts at the Grand. Jesse met Glendinning at Tribeca Games in June and played the game ...
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player

Editor’s note: Our Tribeca 2026 coverage continues with Jesse Rylander’s conversation with Anil Glendinning, co-founder and creative director of Friday Sundae, the studio behind There Are No Ghosts at the Grand. Jesse met Glendinning at Tribeca Games in June and played the game on the gallery floor at Pier 57. What follows is his account.

There Are No Ghosts at the Grand, inside the greenhouse. Courtesy of Friday Sundae.

Some games tell you their genre in a word. There Are No Ghosts at the Grand needs a whole breath. When I sat down with Anil Glendinning at Tribeca Games, he described it, without blinking, as “a musical, narrative, renovation, horror, comedy, story game.” After spending time with it on the gallery floor at Pier 57, I understood why he didn’t bother trimming the list. Every one of those words is doing work.

The setup is simple enough. You play Chris David, an American who inherits a crumbling seaside hotel in England from the British side of a family he has never met. By day, you restore the Grand and the sleepy village around it with a toolkit of increasingly bizarre power tools, some of which talk back. By night, those same tools turn into ghost-hunting gear. There is also a sardonic cat. And, at unpredictable moments, the people of the town break into song.

Glendinning is co-founder and creative director of Friday Sundae, a UK studio of just ten people, and he co-directs the game with producer Rachel Glendinning. The game had its world premiere at Tribeca in June 2026 and won the Tribeca Games Award, the festival’s prize for excellence in artistic storytelling, chosen from 12 official selections.

Our conversation made it clear that nearly every choice in it, from the textures to the soundtrack, traces back to one idea: a ghost story should feel like a memory.

Players at the Tribeca Games gallery, Pier 57, New York. Photo: Jesse Rylander.

A ghost story built from a childhood

When the team began writing, Glendinning said, they went back to the places that had frightened them as kids. Not haunted mansions, but something more specific and more British. “We thought of rainy seaside towns in the UK that are out of season,” he told me. “These weird liminal spaces that are empty of people. Places that are designed for fun but which look frightening at nighttime and in the rain, like fairground rides and deserted amusement arcades.”

If you have ever walked a boardwalk in February, you know exactly the feeling. Kingswood-on-Sea, the fictional town around the Grand, is built out of that mood.

The music came from the same place. Growing up, the team was listening to reggae, ska, and punk from the late 70s and 80s: The Clash, Madness, The Specials, The Selecter. At first, those references were meant only to shape the score. Then something happened that Glendinning describes as almost accidental.

“Almost naturally, almost organically, characters started to sing these words,” he said. “And we found that it felt like a perfect match for this surreal, slightly unsettling environment that we wanted to create.”

The musical numbers are not a break from the horror; they feed it. “There is something a little bit surreal and unsettling about someone singing to you,” Glendinning explained, “and you as a character being aware that they’re singing, but they being completely unaware of it.” That mismatch, he hinted, is part of the mystery itself. There is a reason this town sings, and a reason the cat and the power tools talk.

Painting a half-remembered place

The Grand’s visual world follows the same logic. Friday Sundae chose painted textures over photorealism, giving the hotel and its surroundings the quality of a half-remembered place.

“It naturally came from the idea of trying to capture a memory,” Glendinning said. Something closer to a half-forgotten photograph, or a roughly sketched image you carry around in your head. “The story that we want to tell didn’t match photorealistic graphics. We wanted it to feel ethereal. We wanted it to feel surreal. We wanted it to feel dreamlike.”

To get there, the studio’s artists hand-paint every texture in the game. The characters and environments sit slightly off true, just uncanny enough to keep you uneasy without tipping into caricature. It is a reminder that in game art, as in animation, style is a storytelling decision before it is an aesthetic one. Here the brushwork is the haunting.

There Are No Ghosts at the Grand, the garden and glasshouses. Courtesy of Friday Sundae.

Lyrics that start as poetry

Each character in the Grand sings in their own genre. The town’s young police officer leans into fast-talking reggae, a direct nod to The Clash. Others have their own sounds, matched to who they are.

Glendinning writes the lyrics himself, as part of each character’s story. “For me, it started off very much as poetry,” he said. Those pieces then go to Luke, the game’s musical director, who shapes them into songs and builds the music around their intention. The process, in his words, was organic and collaborative, and frequently ended up somewhere neither of them expected.

His rule for navigating that: “Follow the story, follow the characters, and follow the music, and see what comes out of it. And then trust gamers to really get what it is that we’re trying to do.”

Casting the ghost with the most

Of course, a musical needs voices. For Chris David, the team wanted an actor who could move from sinister and spooky to funny, mysterious, and completely out of control, sometimes within a single scene. They found that range in Alex Brightman, who spent years playing the title role in Beetlejuice on Broadway.

“We reached out to him just on the off chance,” Glendinning said, “and the stars aligned.” Brightman was interested in what the studio was building, and they have been working together ever since. His deep roots in New York theater made a premiere at Tribeca feel like a happy coincidence.

Friday Sundae has also added another familiar voice to the cast: Billy Boyd, best known as Pippin in The Lord of the Rings, plays MacBrushy, a Scottish power tool who talks and, naturally, sings.

There Are No Ghosts at the Grand, a cat and a glowing doorway. Courtesy of Friday Sundae.

A small team, room for surprises

The thread that ties all of this together is ambition at an unusually human scale. Glendinning described Friday Sundae as fully self-funded and self-publishing, with a team of ten. The priority, he said, was to deliver well on a small number of platforms rather than spread thin.

That smallness is also the point creatively. Glendinning looks back fondly at the original Xbox and PS2 era, when 3D genres were still taking shape, and smaller, more agile teams could try strange mechanics just to see if they were fun. He name-checked Viva Piñata, the Clock Tower games, and the early Silent Hill titles as games that genuinely surprised him.

“Today, you buy a game, it’s in the genre, you kind of know what to expect from that,” he said. “So we wanted to create something that was unexpected.” Mechanics and story turns are designed to arrive from angles you won’t anticipate. “If you like surprises,” he told me, “if you like unpredictability, There Are No Ghosts at the Grand is for you.”

The Tribeca Games gallery, Pier 57, New York. Photo: Jesse Rylander.

After my conversation with Glendinning, I keep coming back to that image of an empty arcade in the rain. Plenty of games try to scare you with what is hiding in the dark. This one seems more interested in the strange feeling of a place that was built for joy and then left alone too long. And then, of course, someone starts to sing.

There Are No Ghosts at the Grand is planned to enter Early Access on PC in December 2026. A demo is available now on Steam.

entry.content:

From editor Nikita Didenko:

Strings Cut is an intense kinetic experiment that explores the visual architecture of Hollywood cinema over the past decade. Bound by two uncompromising rules — strict center-framed composition and continuous match-cutting — this 80-second edit orchestrates a seamless flow across 107 different films, synchronized to a frantic, hyper-dynamic violin score.

Instead of a standard montage, the project builds an abstract narrative driven entirely by motion vectors and geometric shapes. The timeline evolves through distinct phases: characters turning from the screen, explosive frontal movements, and hidden visual links between circular geometries found in completely unrelated blockbusters.

Craft & Process

In an era of generative AI, this piece is a testament to human editorial intuition. Every single cut was placed manually, with some shots flashing on screen for a mere 5 frames to match the accelerating BPM of the soundtrack. Sourcing and mapping thousands of individual shots required a meticulous hybrid workflow, combining the shot-logging platform Shotdeck with hundreds of hours of manual, frame-by-frame film analysis.

entry.title: The Flowers Look Back: teamLab at OFFF Barcelona 2026
entry.summary: Editor’s note: Our OFFF Barcelona 2026 conversations continue. Following Onur Senturk on the compulsion to create , Tim Thompson of RevThink sits down with Sakurako “Saka” Naka of teamLab, the Tokyo art collective behind Borderless and Phenomena, the morning after her talk on the...
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player

Editor’s note: Our OFFF Barcelona 2026 conversations continue. Following Onur Senturk on the compulsion to create, Tim Thompson of RevThink sits down with Sakurako “Saka” Naka of teamLab, the Tokyo art collective behind Borderless and Phenomena, the morning after her talk on the main stage. What follows is Tim’s account of the conversation.

Saka arrived with a laptop and an apology. “I didn’t prepare myself at all,” she said, “because I think it’s very uninteresting, for the most part.” We were outside Disseny Hub on the last morning of the festival, in the sun, a few hours before she had to be back on a plane to Tokyo. By the time an OFFF producer came to find her, nearly an hour later, I had stopped asking questions and she had stopped apologizing.

I came to the conversation wanting to understand a structure. How does an art collective become big enough to open permanent museums on three continents without turning into a company, or at least without feeling like one? I left with something closer to a philosophy of making, and with a standing invitation to Tokyo that I intend to use.

teamLab, Universe of Water Particles on a Rock where People Gather. teamLab Borderless, Tokyo. © teamLab

A laboratory for a team

The story begins about 25 years ago with five friends leaving graduate school. One of them, Toshiyuki Inoko, whom everyone at teamLab calls Toshi, wanted to make things. “Art 25 years ago is not sustainable,” Saka said, then caught herself. “It’s not even now.” So by day the five built technology for companies, and whatever revenue came in went into artworks. “That’s how we self-sustained.”

That arrangement never went away. It grew into two pillars. One side, which they call digital solutions, builds apps and systems for postal services, banks, and airlines, and now works at a nationwide scale in Japan. The other side is the art collective. Three of the four friends who started with Toshi are still there, and they run the digital solutions side “so that Toshi can just focus on making things.”

The name is literal. “When teamLab started, the reason why it’s called teamLab is, it’s a laboratory for a team.” I asked whether that made the team the experiment. She laughed. “Not necessarily a human experiment.”

Nobody has a title

I tried to find the org chart and could not. When I asked whether Toshi functioned as a creative director, Saka paused over the comparison. “I honestly don’t know what creative directors are. We don’t have titles within teamLab.” What they have instead is what she calls a gathering of specialists. Artists, but also mathematicians, software and hardware engineers, architects, and a botanical team. “Are you serious?” I asked. She was. They work with living flowers.

Work forms around an artwork, not around a department. An idea begins, often with Toshi, and the group that gathers around it evolves by need: which specialty is required to make this, who should be experimenting on it. Some of those series have been running for more than 15 years, each iteration asking the same question in a new form, such as whether light can become a three-dimensional sculpture in space. “We’re always interested in just keeping on making,” she said. An exhibition is the moment to ask what the team is interested in right now, and what it wants to show.

When a museum or exhibition approaches, a different kind of member steps in. “We have these members called catalysts,” she said. “They bring everyone together.” I pointed out that this sounded like a title. “It’s more of an adjective.” The catalyst knows every engineer and architect working on every artwork and pulls them into the plan for the larger space.

“We don’t have titles within teamLab.”

Everyone is full time. “It’s not a drop-in, drop-out situation, because there’s always something to be making.” And the wall between the two pillars is porous. If an artwork needs an insight that lives on the digital solutions side, someone walks over. “People make friends.”

teamLab Borderless, MORI Building Digital Art Museum, Azabudai Hills, Tokyo. © teamLab

Every piece of wood is different

teamLab does everything in-house, from the first experiment to the last projector. Artworks start small in the Tokyo studio, scale up in large warehouses far outside the city, and get finished on site, where the team spends weeks working out corners and angles. “There’s so much you discover just using your hands to do things,” Saka said. “You never really know until you’re physically in the space.”

The discovery does not stay with one person. It is shared across the team and carried into the next artwork, so the knowledge compounds. Her example for this had nothing to do with projectors. In old Japanese architecture, she said, the craftsmen who shaved the wooden beams for the great temples were also part of deciding what the structure would look like. “Every piece of wood is different. So the people working with the actual material could also have an input in the larger structure.” That separation came later. “It’s not whether it’s good or bad. It’s just something different that has happened.”

The Tokyo studio is built to keep that input flowing. One floor is entirely open, a lot of tables and no walls, with only two glassed rooms so that overseas calls are possible. Everyone is working on several things at once, so when a question about a space comes up in a meeting, the person who can answer it is usually within reach. “You can tap someone over very easily.”

Somewhere in here I offered her my starfish metaphor, the one about a creature with no brain whose parts still agree on a direction, and how a whole school of them will move together with no visible way of communicating. She was polite about it. “In some of our artworks there are schools of fish. Or birds. It’s some communication that we don’t fully understand. There’s so much that we don’t know.”

The flowers look back

Then she opened the laptop, and the conversation stopped being about structure.

She showed me the garden first. More than 13,000 living orchids fill a room in Tokyo, suspended in the air with no soil, because most orchids can absorb water from the air. “They found another way to live on this planet,” she said. When you walk in, the flowers hang low. Stand still, and the ones around you begin to float upward, opening a space around your body. Walk slowly and the space moves with you. If someone enters from the other side, your two spaces merge.

teamLab, Floating Flower Garden: Flowers and I are of the Same Root, the Garden and I are One, 2015-, interactive installation. © teamLab

The work comes from a Zen saying about looking at a flower as though looking at a dream. “We know in our brains that we’re connected to nature,” she said. “But it’s difficult to recognize it as that.” The orchids are the attempt. “If you stand for a while, the flowers almost look back at you.”

“If you stand for a while, the flowers almost look back at you.”

teamLab, Floating Flower Garden. More than 13,000 living orchids, rooted in air. © teamLab

You cannot put a whirlpool in a box

Earlier I had given her a theory of mine about the four stages of a creative career, which ends with the collector, the person whose value lies in what they gather. Saka came back to it an hour later with a better answer than mine, and it started with a whirlpool.

Humans, she said, have mostly made objects. Our cities are full of them. But in the south of Japan, where Toshi grew up, there are some of the largest whirlpools in the world, and a whirlpool is not an object. The water inside it is exactly the same as the water outside it. What makes it exist is an order of energy, a flow passing through. “You could not scoop it up and put it in a silver box. It would stop existing the moment you tried.”

teamLab, Light Vortex. teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi. © teamLab

That idea became a series called Environmental Phenomena, and a building. teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi, developed with the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi and Miral, is full of sculptures that are made by the environment itself: a column of spheres that rises about five meters and reads as a solid vertical form from across the room, held up by nothing but air flow. You can walk into it and it keeps existing. You cannot take it home. “It’s inseparable from the environment,” Saka said. “As long as this environment exists, these sculptures will continue to emerge.” I asked who at teamLab commissioned the content. “We decided everything that went in there.”

teamLab, Morphing Continuum. A sculpture of spheres held in place by the flow of air alone. teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi. © teamLab

No map

Borderless, teamLab’s permanent museum in Tokyo, moved into a new space in 2024, and the next one is going to Hamburg. There is no map and no route. You walk in and out of rooms and stay as long as you like, and the artworks do the same. They leave one room, travel the corridors, take another form, and overlap with each other. They also respond to whoever is there. The butterflies are born from people, so at the start of the day, before anyone arrives, there are no butterflies. Touch one and it dies. “It’s just one world,” she said, “and it depends on who’s there with you and how they’re behaving.”

teamLab, Flutter of Butterflies Beyond Borders. teamLab Borderless, Tokyo. © teamLab

This is where she talked about beauty, and it is the line I keep returning to. People usually call something beautiful when it has been separated from the rest of the world, a single flower, a single ring. Inside Borderless, where everything is changing because of you and because of the strangers beside you, that reflex falls away. “At one point you start to feel like it’s the whole that’s beautiful. The fact that the world is continuous, and that we live in this continuity, that’s the object of beauty.”

“The fact that the world is continuous, and that we live in this continuity, that’s the object of beauty.”

I thought of a field of poppies. You can photograph it, or pick one flower and carry it home, and either might be lovely on its own. Neither is the field. The field includes its scale, its surroundings, and the fact that you were standing in it.

A different way of seeing

The last thing she showed me was a wall of blooming flowers, and the hardest idea of the hour. Most of what we look at now has passed through a lens, and a lens fixes a point of view. “When your perspective is fixed, you don’t need your body,” she said. That is not a bad thing, she was careful to add. It made objectivity possible. But teamLab has spent years on the opposite problem: how to turn something three-dimensional into two dimensions without discarding the body, so that what you see feels like it shares your space.

teamLab, People Don’t See the World as through a Camera. The letters at the entrance of teamLab Borderless only rise toward you through a lens. © teamLab

They call the answer Ultrasubjective Space, a logical construct for flattening a scene without fixing the viewer’s eye. In the room, you cannot tell whether the flowers are blooming on your side of the wall or beyond it, and people drift toward them without deciding to. I kept asking about the mechanism, whether there were layered planes, whether something moved. She kept returning me to how the image was built. “People don’t look at the world like a lens does in the first place.” Pre-modern East Asian scrolls and folding screens, she pointed out, were never drawn in Western perspective. “It’s probably just how they saw.” When I asked whether this was a technical breakthrough or a creative one, she gave the most teamLab answer of the morning. “Sometimes things just don’t exist, and we just have to make it up.”

teamLab, Flowers and People, Cannot be Controlled but Live Together. teamLab Borderless, Tokyo. © teamLab

Today, then tomorrow

I spend my working life with creative business owners, and most of them are being taught, including by the speakers at this festival, how to become commercial artists. teamLab did it the other way around. They built a commercial engine so the art would never have to ask permission, and 25 years later the engine is still running and the art is still the point.

People ask Toshi about his plans in five years, in ten. Saka says the answer never changes. “I just want to keep making something today. And then tomorrow, and the day after, and I’ll just keep doing that.” She smiled. “And then one day I’ll die.”

That sounds like a plan. The OFFF film crew came for her a minute later. She gave me her number for Tokyo, and I have never been to Tokyo. She is going to be the reason.

“I just want to keep making something today. And then tomorrow, and the day after.”

teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi, Saadiyat Cultural District. © teamLab

Interview and words: Tim Thompson, RevThink, recorded at OFFF Barcelona 2026

entry.title: Sekondo Puts ChatGPT and Claude Inside After Effects and Premiere Pro.
entry.summary: Córdoba-based graphic designer Jose Manuel Fernández has launched Sekondo, a plugin that connects ChatGPT and Claude to six Adobe applications: After Effects, Premiere Pro, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Lightroom Classic. Instead of generating new images or clips, the AI w...
entry.content:
Córdoba-based graphic designer Jose Manuel Fernández has launched Sekondo, a plugin that connects ChatGPT and Claude to six Adobe applications: After Effects, Premiere Pro, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Lightroom Classic.

Instead of generating new images or clips, the AI works inside the artist’s own project. You describe what you need, typed or spoken, and it applies the changes to your layers, keyframes, compositions and timelines, with everything left editable.
Like at any studio, a good part of Fernández’s day went into repetitive work: adapting a piece to twenty formats, versioning, building the same lower thirds again and again.

“These tasks are necessary, but they eat up hours I’d rather spend thinking up an idea. I built Sekondo to have more time to design.”

In Premiere Pro and After Effects, Sekondo can edit, animate and finish complete pieces with the artist’s own footage and under their direction, from the first cut to complex motion. Rather than handing back a finished clip that can’t be changed, it reads how a project is built, measures before it acts and keeps every layer editable.
The artist decides how far it goes: carrying out instructions, suggesting ideas and options, or building a whole piece from their idea. Files never leave the user’s computer.

Sekondo is published on Adobe Exchange, Adobe’s official marketplace for these apps, after passing Adobe’s review. It runs on macOS and Windows with the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps.

entry.content:
ROVE has launched a new brand identity and website, reflecting its evolution from a two-person live-action shop into a design, animation and motion-led creative studio. The launch also marks its signing with Ashley McKim Consulting for strategic sales and marketing across brands and agencies.

Founded in Portland, Maine, in 2017 by Gabe Bornstein and Jay Brown, ROVE now works with a remote team across the U.S. and Canada. The name stays ROVE; “Beyond” expresses the studio’s approach to moving between disciplines, from design and animation to live action, VFX and production.

“We’ve grown into a studio driven by design and animation, and it was time for our brand to tell that story,” says Brown. “We don’t want to be defined by a single style or discipline.”

Built in partnership with STOKT, the website brings together a new showreel and expanded case studies for clients including Google, NOBULL and Spotify. Projects open up the studio’s process across design, animation, live action and finishing, while playful details extend to an interactive mini-game on the 404 page.

ROVE’s in-house creative team led the rebrand, working with a wider group of collaborators. Irene Feleo collaborated on the wordmark and core stamp, with other artists contributing their own stamp interpretations. Connor Linde contributed to elements of the brand identity. The studio carried the system through its website art direction, motion identity, showreel and presentation materials.

Ashley McKim Consulting joins ROVE’s existing representation by Aspire Artists Agency, which continues to focus on broadcast and streaming entertainment. ROVE’s work in that space includes Disney and Freeform’s 25 Days of Christmas. The studio’s broader client list includes Toyota, Converse and NOBULL.
